measurement.happened:
This week in China was dominated by several major threads running in parallel.

The most dramatic single event was the magnitude 7 earthquake that struck Tibet on October 22, killing at least 16 people and injuring 76, with hundreds of homes collapsed. Rescuers were still searching for survivors as of October 23. This was the largest seismic event in the region in years and added to a year in which China's natural disaster losses had already hit $30 billion in the first nine months (Reuters, AP, CNN, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg).

On the economic front, China reported third-quarter GDP growth of 4.5 percent, narrowly beating forecasts and accelerating from the prior quarter, driven primarily by robust exports, particularly in AI hardware and technology. However, domestic demand remained weak, foreign direct investment fell 4.3 percent year-over-year, and consumer confidence continued to erode. The stock market told a bleaker story: the CSI 300 extended a 10-week losing streak, pushing Chinese equities deeper into bear-market territory despite state buying. AI-model-related stocks alone shed an estimated $150 billion in value with no sign of stabilization. Bridgewater cut its gold allocation and turned cautiously optimistic on local stocks, while sovereign wealth funds surged 190 percent into China and Hong Kong positions after a bruising slump. Citi finally won its long-awaited license to set up a fully owned securities unit in China after nearly five years of waiting, a symbolic win for foreign market access. Evergrande's liquidators, after two and a half years, recovered just 1 percent of debt claims, underscoring the slow grind of the property sector's unwinding. China also urged oil and gas companies to boost output and build strategic supply bases, and its copper smelters planned further output cuts ahead of fee negotiations. The country snapped up Australian canola as improved bilateral ties and lower tariffs fueled demand, while Rio Tinto and China's state buyer agreed on an iron ore supply deal. Meanwhile, Fortescue warned of possible operations disruption as the China state-buyer talks dragged on, and Japan was reportedly months from running out of a critical rare earth as China squeezed supply.

Artificial intelligence was arguably the defining theme of the week. DeepSeek, the Chinese AI startup, raised $15 billion in a funding round ahead of a potential IPO, positioning itself to challenge top US AI labs. The US Treasury proposed a rule to crack down on high-tech investments in China and other adversaries, and separately banned DeepSeek from use in government agency systems, a move Beijing called discriminatory. China pushed back, defending DeepSeek and urging the US to stop targeting Chinese research institutions. MiniMax completed export registration for its open-source AI model for overseas licensing. The HKEX launched new AI and semiconductor indexes. China's first fully AI-generated feature film hit cinemas, though ticket sales lagged. The government urged agencies to mitigate AI job displacement. CNN explored whether China was using AI tokens mostly to produce micro-dramas. Bloomberg reported that Beijing had mixed feelings about DeepSeek's push for ubiquity. Alibaba shares posted their steepest drop in two months amid new regulatory curbs. The broader narrative was one of a US-China AI rivalry intensifying while China's domestic AI ecosystem matured rapidly.

The trade and industrial competition with the West sharpened. The EU vowed to address what it called 'China Shock 2.0' through talks with Beijing, looking beyond autos for the next round of negotiations. Volvo Cars plunged 24 percent after its CEO declared that China's market was effectively gone for Western automakers and that Europe-developed models would not work there. Gucci and Hermès both reported disappointing sales, citing a challenging backdrop in China. Bosch announced it would separate its auto-parts unit as Chinese rivals gained ground. Chinese automakers BYD, Chery, and others accelerated overseas production plans, with BYD doubling capacity in Brazil and Chery eyeing Canada. European car sales growth accelerated as Chinese brands seized market share. The EU also proposed curbs on Chinese hybrid vehicles, which could make European automakers more investable. TSMC sought factory-equipment alternatives to reduce dependence on China's rare-earth grip. Chinese battery makers raced to invest abroad to avoid Western barriers.

In diplomacy, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un made an unannounced visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong on October 24, crossing a newly opened cross-border bridge, signaling warming trade and political ties. Trump said he was ready to meet with both Putin and Xi in China, and the Kremlin confirmed China was preparing for a possible trilateral meeting on Ukraine, though the three leaders would sit at one table without Ukraine itself. China's foreign minister urged stronger international governance of the deep sea and outer space and opposed an arms race in space. China and Djibouti jointly called for freedom of navigation in the Red Sea. South Africa's trade with China surged after a duty-free deal.

On the Taiwan front, Taipei said China was using militia boats to expand what it called 'battlefield preparation' in the western Pacific. Taiwan indicted five people accused of transnational repression linked to mocking Xi. Sixteen Chinese ships were involved in what Taiwan described as maritime harassment operations. The Philippines summoned the Chinese ambassador over remarks it said threatened force. China's coast guard monitored a Philippine resupply vessel at a disputed shoal.

The Communist Party's fifth plenum was set for October 26 to 29, with early reporting emphasizing tougher internal discipline and consolidation of Xi's authority. The plenum is expected to set the direction for the next five-year economic and political plan.

Other notable items: a nursery owner in China was jailed for life after hundreds of children were poisoned; the FBI arrested a woman accused of spying for China; Chinese-linked hackers compromised ConnectWise in a global attack; the US blocked two devices containing Chinese-made surveillance chips; a House committee said Webull messages pointed to Chinese access to US customer data; China's economy was described as barely easing austerity just before a shift to stimulus mode; wealthy Chinese were moving offshore money to US banks as Beijing's tax net widened; China's luxury brands were seen as ready to elbow Western rivals aside; the second-hand luxury market was booming; and Tropical Storm Champi, after battering Taiwan and Japan, was on a path toward mainland China.

In sports, China's women's gymnastics team edged out the US for world team gold, and golfer Yin won back-to-back LPGA titles in Shanghai.
measurement.expected:
The single most important event of next week is the fifth plenum of the Communist Party of China, running October 26 to 29. This is almost certain to produce a formal communiqué laying out the economic and political priorities for the next five-year period, with emphasis on qualitative growth, technological self-reliance, and internal discipline. Expect the plenum to be the dominant story in Chinese and international media, with analysts parsing every sentence for signals on stimulus, AI policy, and the balance between state and market. Confidence: almost certain the plenum happens as scheduled and produces a communiqué; probable that it signals a modest shift toward more stimulus and consumer support, given the domestic weakness highlighted by Q3 data.

Tropical Storm Champi is expected to make landfall or pass close to China's eastern or southern coast in the next few days. This is almost certain to bring heavy rain, wind, and possible flooding to coastal provinces, with follow-up reporting on damage, evacuations, and transport disruptions. Confidence: almost certain the storm affects China in some form; possible that it causes significant disruption to ports and shipping lanes, which would compound the already-stressed trade environment.

The Kim Jong Un visit to Dandong will generate follow-up coverage, including any joint statements, photos of bilateral meetings, and commentary on the warming North Korea-China axis. Expect this to be framed in the context of the broader US-China-Russia triangle, especially with the possible Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral meeting in the offing. Confidence: almost certain there will be follow-up diplomatic messaging; possible that a joint statement on trade or security is issued; unlikely that the visit produces a major new agreement within the week.

The stock market is in bear territory after a 10-week slide. The plenum's outcome will be the key catalyst. If it signals stronger stimulus, a relief rally is possible but likely to be short-lived given the $150 billion in AI-stock losses and fading policy hopes. If it is more cautious, the slide continues. Confidence: probable that the plenum provides a short-term sentiment boost; possible that the bear market extends further if stimulus announcements are seen as insufficient.

The US-China AI rivalry will continue to escalate. The US Treasury's proposed rule on high-tech investments, the DeepSeek government ban, and the broader tech-investment curbs will generate further headlines. Expect China to respond with its own regulatory or diplomatic moves, possibly including new restrictions on US tech in China or accelerated open-source AI push. Confidence: probable that at least one new US or Chinese AI-related policy move lands in the next week; possible that DeepSeek or MiniMake makes a significant product or funding announcement.

EU-China trade talks will continue, with the 'China Shock 2.0' narrative driving the agenda. The EU is looking beyond autos, so expect discussions on batteries, semiconductors, and possibly services. Confidence: probable that the EU and China hold or schedule a working-level meeting; possible that a specific sector (e.g., EVs or semiconductors) becomes the focus of a new round of negotiations.

The rare-earth and mineral squeeze will remain a live issue, with Japan's supply concerns and the US Treasury's biotech investment curbs adding pressure. Expect China to use its leverage in iron ore, copper, and rare earths as a bargaining chip in trade talks. Confidence: probable that at least one new commodity or trade-related headline emerges; unlikely that a full resolution of the rare-earth dispute happens within the week.

The pharma and biotech sector will continue to be a bright spot, with the GLP-1 market boom, the Roche-Hansoh deal, and China's rapid human-trial pipeline drawing Western attention. Expect more partnership announcements or regulatory approvals. Confidence: possible that one or two additional pharma deals or approvals are announced; unlikely that the sector becomes a headline driver compared to AI and trade.

Less likely surprises: a significant new US sanction or export control targeting a specific Chinese tech firm beyond DeepSeek; a major new Chinese stimulus package announced outside the plenum; a second earthquake or natural disaster in a different region; a sudden shift in the yuan exchange rate that triggers a new round of market volatility; a major corporate scandal or accounting issue at a large Chinese listed company. Confidence in each: possible to unlikely.

Things I would not bet on: a full US-China trade truce or tariff rollback within the week; a major Chinese military exercise or live-fire drill in the Taiwan Strait beyond routine operations; the Communist Party plenum producing a dramatic break from the current economic model; China announcing a new space launch or deep-sea mission that dominates the news cycle; a new Chinese property developer default or restructuring announcement of the scale of Evergrande; the yuan hitting a new multi-year low or high within the next seven days.

delta.motion: The most dramatic growth between the two photographs is in the US-China AI rivalry, which went from a one-sided story (China drafting export controls on AI models and chips) to a full two-way confrontation: DeepSeek raised fifteen billion dollars ahead of a possible IPO, the US Treasury proposed a rule to crack down on high-tech investments in China, Washington banned DeepSeek from government systems, MiniMax completed its export registration for overseas licensing, and the US blocked two devices containing Chinese-made surveillance chips. AI also moved into culture, with China's first fully AI-generated feature film hitting cinemas, and into market infrastructure, as the HKEX launched new AI and semiconductor indexes. The stock market story worsened sharply: what was described as a 'wobble' in the first week became a ten-week losing streak for the CSI 300, pushing equities deeper into bear-market territory, with AI-model stocks alone shedding an estimated one hundred fifty billion dollars. The EU-China trade friction also grew from 'additional sectors beyond autos' to a formal 'China Shock 2.0' framing, with the EU proposing curbs on Chinese hybrid vehicles, Volvo's CEO declaring the Chinese market effectively gone for Western automakers, and luxury brands like Gucci and Hermès reporting disappointing Chinese sales. The North Korea relationship deepened from the symbolic bridge opening to Kim Jong Un personally crossing the new bridge into Dandong, a concrete diplomatic act that went beyond the 'more analysis than news' the first week suggested. The US-China financial-access story resolved in one direction: Citi finally won its long-awaited license for a fully owned securities unit, a concrete concession that was only hinted at in the first week. New themes that appeared and had no counterpart in the first photograph include the magnitude-seven Tibet earthquake, the fifth Party plenum set for late October, the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral meeting possibility on Ukraine, the Evergrande liquidation update showing only one percent recovery after two and a half years, the Tropical Storm Champi approaching the mainland, a cluster of cyber-espionage stories (ConnectWise hack, Webull messages, FBI spy arrest), and the Japan rare-earth shortage warning. delta.wind: The expectation that APEC would dominate the diplomatic calendar was largely wrong. The second photograph shows the fifth Party plenum (October 26-29) as the major upcoming event, and the Tibet earthquake as the week's biggest single story. APEC may have taken place but did not generate the headline dominance predicted. The expectation of formalized AI export controls was partially right: MiniMax completed export registration and the broader AI policy framework moved forward, but the story evolved into a two-way US-China AI rivalry (DeepSeek ban, Treasury rule, surveillance chips) rather than a one-sided Chinese regulatory announcement. The EU trade proposal expectation was right and then some: the EU moved to 'China Shock 2.0' talks and proposed curbs on hybrid vehicles, broader than the auto-sector focus anticipated. The stock market volatility call was directionally correct but understated: a ten-week losing streak and a one-hundred-fifty-billion-dollar AI stock wipeout go well beyond 'volatility and further intervention.' The yuan-strengthening expectation faded; the yuan is barely mentioned in the second photograph, suggesting the story stalled or was absorbed into broader trade dynamics. The anti-corruption and tax-enforcement expectation held: the nursery owner's life sentence was confirmed, and wealthy Chinese were actively moving money to US banks as Beijing's tax net widened. The Philippines friction expectation was accurate: the ambassador was summoned, the coast guard monitored a resupply vessel, but no new naval incident occurred, exactly as predicted. The US-China bilateral talks expectation was right in a specific way: Citi's securities-unit license is the 'narrow concession' that was anticipated, and the broader financial-access story (Mastercard, Citigroup) resolved at least in part. The North Korea bridge expectation of 'more analysis than news' was wrong in the best way: Kim Jong Un physically crossed the bridge into Dandong, turning a follow-up story into a concrete diplomatic event. The 'less likely' surprise of a major tech IPO was closer to reality than predicted: DeepSeek's fifteen-billion-dollar raise ahead of a potential IPO is not a full listing, but it is a significant capital event. The 'would not bet on' list was most notably violated by the Tibet earthquake, a major natural disaster that was explicitly listed as unlikely. The plenum, the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral possibility, the Evergrande one-percent recovery, the surveillance-chip cluster, and the Japan rare-earth warning all appeared without being in the expectations. The biggest pattern of error is that the expectations treated the week as a continuation of the previous week's themes at slightly higher intensity, when in fact the week introduced genuinely new structural events (earthquake, plenum, trilateral meeting, DeepSeek's capital raise) and resolved some threads (Citi license, nursery sentencing) while making others more dramatic (AI rivalry, EU trade framing, stock market decline). The expectations underweighted the possibility of a one-off shock event and overweighted the smooth continuation of policy threads.
delta.driver: The central force pushing China from the first photograph to the second is the accelerating collision between its ambition to lead the global AI and technology order and the increasingly coordinated resistance of the US and EU to that leadership. China is not just restricting its own exports; it is building a full-stack domestic AI ecosystem (DeepSeek, MiniMax, AI film, AI indexes) while simultaneously absorbing US containment measures (Treasury rules, DeepSeek ban, surveillance-chip blocks), forcing it into a defensive-offensive posture where every US move triggers a Chinese counter. Domestically, the weak consumer demand, the ten-week stock market slide, and the property sector's slow unwinding (Evergrande at one percent) are squeezing the government's policy space, pushing it toward the fifth plenum as the mechanism to set a coherent five-year direction that balances stimulus, structural reform, and political consolidation. The North Korea deepening and the possible Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral on Ukraine show Beijing using multilateral and bilateral channels to position itself as an indispensable mediator while its bilateral relationships with the US and EU grow more adversarial. The Tibet earthquake and Tropical Storm Champi add a recurring domestic pressure that tests governance and resource allocation. Underneath all of this is a simple arithmetic problem: China's export engine is strong (forty-five percent growth, AI hardware driving it), but the domestic demand engine is weak, foreign investment is falling, and the stock market is in a prolonged bear run, meaning the government must either open up more (Citi license, financial market access) or stimulate more aggressively (the 'shift to stimulus mode' the second photograph hints at), while simultaneously defending its technological position against two Western blocs that are coordinating more tightly than a week earlier.

Think of it like the school board meeting that sets the rules for the next five years. The leaders will talk about how to help the economy grow more, especially because people at home are not spending as much money as before, and they will probably say something encouraging about the stock market, which has been falling for ten weeks straight. They will also talk about making sure the AI companies, like DeepSeek, get government support because the US and Europe are trying to slow China down in that area.

China is mad and will probably push back with its own rules or complaints. It is a bit like two neighbors arguing over who gets to use the shared driveway, except the driveway is the global tech market.

On top of all that, a big earthquake hit Tibet earlier this week, killing at least 16 people and destroying hundreds of homes. Rescuers are still searching for survivors, and a tropical storm is heading toward the mainland. So the government has to juggle the big political meeting, the trade arguments with the US and Europe, the stock market worries, and the disaster response all at the same time. It is a lot to handle in one week, and the news will be busy.
